 How AI Could Help Cambodia Predict and Prevent Dengue Outbreaks
 Dengue patients in Kantha Bopha's children's hospital. Photo by Kantha Bopha 
 By:
 Sonny Inbaraj Krishnan
 November 19, 2026 ,
 7:15 PM 
 00:00 / 00:00 
 PHNOM PENH – A new report by the World Health Organization (WHO) says artificial intelligence and climate data could help countries predict disease outbreaks before they happen, giving health authorities more time to prepare. For Cambodia, where dengue remains a recurring public health challenge, the findings point to an opportunity to strengthen surveillance and identify high-risk areas before cases begin to rise.
 The report, Artificial Intelligence in Climate Adaptation and Health: Emerging Use Cases and Considerations for the Western Pacific Region , examines how countries are using data and predictive tools to respond to health risks linked to climate change.
 Dengue is one of the diseases receiving particular attention. Transmission is closely linked to temperature, rainfall and humidity, while long-running surveillance systems provide the historical case data needed to develop forecasting models.
 As of July 12, 2026, Cambodia recorded 28,074 dengue fever cases and 38 deaths, marking a 58.1 percent increase compared to the same period in 2025. Climate change has caused a phenomenal rise in dengue cases . Rising temperatures accelerate mosquito development and allow the dengue virus to multiply faster inside mosquitoes, while changing rainfall patterns create more breeding sites.
 But the WHO-WPRO report makes an important distinction: predicting an outbreak is not the same as preventing one. Forecasts only become useful when health authorities know who should act, when a response should begin and what measures need to be taken.
 Lessons From the Region 
 Some countries in the region are already showing what climate-informed dengue surveillance can achieve.
 Singapore offers one of the clearest examples . Since 2013, the National Environment Agency, working with local universities, has used a machine-learning model to forecast dengue cases up to three months ahead.
 In one early test, the model predicted in March that weekly cases would peak at about 800 in June. The actual peak reached 842 cases.
 The forecasts have helped authorities prepare hospital beds, ensure diagnostic capacity, mobilize ground teams for mosquito source reduction and organize public education campaigns before case numbers climb.
 The value of the system lies not only in its ability to predict cases but also in the way the forecasts are connected to decisions and public health responses.
 China has also developed dengue forecasting models using weekly surveillance data, weather conditions and online search activity. A study in Guangdong province compared six modeling approaches and found that support vector regression performed best. The researchers also tested the model against data from other provinces.
 In the Philippines , researchers developed a machine-learning model to predict dengue incidence in metropolitan Manila using local weather information. The WHO report says the work provides a foundation for stronger forecasting, but identifies further steps needed to connect predictions with the health authorities responsible for responding.
 These examples show that forecasting can help countries prepare earlier. They also underline the importance of building a clear link between information and action.
 Where Cambodia Stands 
 Cambodia is not yet using an operational artificial intelligence system to forecast dengue outbreaks, according to the WHO report. It places the country among those modernizing surveillance systems while research into climate-related health risks continues.
 The report points to Cambodian research showing how remotely sensed flood indicators can contribute to early warning for leptospirosis, a disease associated with flooding. It also notes the country's climate and health resilience program.
 These efforts offer a starting point. They show that climate information can be used to strengthen disease surveillance, even before more advanced forecasting systems are introduced.
 The Lao People's Democratic Republic provides a nearby example of the next step. It is integrating climate data into its national health information system , DHIS2, while piloting a climate-informed early warning and response system for dengue and diarrheal diseases.
 Cambodia could draw lessons from this approach by building on existing health information and surveillance systems rather than starting with an expensive, stand-alone artificial intelligence platform.
 The first priority should be reliable data. Dengue case reports need to be timely, consistent and detailed enough to show where infections are occurring. These records can then be combined with rainfall, temperature, humidity and local environmental information to identify patterns that may signal rising transmission.
 From Forecasts to Action 
 One of the report's strongest messages is that technology alone will not improve public health responses.
 Across the 50 records reviewed, only seven had embedded adaptation directly into their analytical models, validation processes, decision pathways or implementation. The report found that many initiatives were generating useful information without clearly showing how it would be used in practice.
 This is a warning for Cambodia. A forecasting model may identify a likely increase in dengue cases, but its value will be limited if provincial health departments do not receive the information in time, lack resources to respond or are unclear about what action is expected.
 A workable system would need agreed alert thresholds and clear responsibilities. If forecasts indicate that cases are likely to rise in a particular district, local health teams should know when to intensify mosquito control, check hospital readiness, inform communities and increase surveillance.
 The forecasts should also be specific enough to help authorities identify neighborhoods at risk. Provincial averages can hide local outbreaks, particularly in densely populated communities where mosquito breeding sites and exposure may vary from one area to another.
 Community reporting can strengthen this picture. Residents, village health volunteers and local health workers may notice changes that are not immediately visible in routine facility-based reports. Their observations can help authorities identify potential hotspots, provided reports are checked and linked to the formal surveillance system.
 Making Surveillance Work for Everyone 
 The WHO report also raises concerns about equity. Across the wider climate and health evidence reviewed, 34 of the 50 records did not explicitly identify vulnerable populations, while 40 did not address equity implications.
 These figures are not specific to dengue research, but they point to a wider problem. Forecasting systems can overlook communities if the data used to build them do not reflect where people live, their access to health services or their exposure to environmental risks.
 Cambodia should therefore make sure that surveillance improvements include rural communities and people living in areas with limited access to health facilities. Local health workers and communities need to be part of the system, not simply recipients of warnings produced elsewhere.
 Indonesia's National Dengue Action Plan for 2026–2029, which includes integrated surveillance and early warning as one of its four pillars, offers another regional example of how dengue forecasting can be linked to national planning.
 For Cambodia, the opportunity is to take a gradual approach. Health authorities could begin by improving the quality and timeliness of existing dengue data, linking them with weather and environmental information, and testing forecasting methods in selected high-risk areas.
 The results would need to be checked against actual case patterns before any model is expanded nationally. The system would also require trained staff, clear oversight and regular funding to keep it working.
 Artificial intelligence will not replace field surveillance, mosquito control or the work of health professionals. Nor can weather data alone explain every change in dengue transmission.
 But used carefully, forecasting could give Cambodia something that conventional surveillance often cannot: more time to act.
 The aim should not simply be to count people who have fallen ill. It should be to identify where the next outbreak may occur, alert the people responsible for responding and help communities prepare before cases surge.
